scenes.narration: This is Open Med Check: an open-source prescribing check for emergency doctors, that reads the doctor's note and the patient's history.

Emergency doctors write orders under time pressure. Two things are easy to miss: a suspicion written only in today's note, before anything is coded, and one past event buried in a long medical history. Most coded-data checks we looked at don't read free text, and clinicians override between about half and ninety-six percent of medication alerts, so a real one can get lost.

Open Med Check runs Gemma 4, an open-weight model that can run on a hospital's own hardware. Gemma reads the note and the history, and cited rules decide. When nothing conflicts, it stays silent. Let's see two synthetic patients.

Bed three: chest pain, a suspected acute coronary syndrome written in today's note, and daily aspirin. The doctor orders dexketoprofen, an anti-inflammatory. The suspected A C S is not coded yet, so the rules alone see no problem.

Gemma reads the note and quotes it. Code checks every quote word for word, and the rules decide: blocked, with the doctor's own words as the evidence, and an alternative the rules have already re-checked.
One click re-checks paracetamol: no issue found by these checks.

Bed five: a wrist sprain after a bicycle fall, normal labs, and ibuprofen for the pain. Today's visit looks routine. But one line in his long past medical history matters: an upper G I bleed from a duodenal ulcer, in twenty twenty-one.

Gemma finds that line, and code checks the quote word for word. A new rule, not yet specialist-reviewed, raises an amber warning that quotes the history, highlighted where it was written. Paracetamol is offered, with no dose until that review. The prescriber still decides.

The model can raise a verdict, never lower it. A past event never counts as a current one, and a denial or a relative's history is dropped. If the model is down, the card says the free text was not checked, instead of looking like a pass.

On seventy-six synthetic cases we wrote ourselves, a development set and not a clinical validation, reading the note lifts the match from seventy-two to ninety-seven percent, with no false alarm on the cases that should stay silent. These figures were measured before we added the history step, which is not yet measured.

Because Gemma's weights are open, the note never has to leave the building. We think the buyer is the hospital's medication-safety team, paying for a maintained rule table, integration and support. That is a hypothesis we have yet to test.

Open Med Check: Gemma reads the note and the history; the rules decide. Today it is a demonstrator on synthetic patients, not a medical device. Next, we are looking for a clinical pilot with a hospital pharmacy. It's open source, on GitHub.
